## M4-E01

**Index the title column** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L273-286](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“That's a savings of almost eight times.”*, [lecture5 L297-316](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“using the index that we called title_index”*

```sql
CREATE INDEX "title_index" ON "movies" ("title");
```

**Why:** SCAN means reading every row top to bottom. SEARCH means using a structure to jump to matching rows.
On the full 400k-row IMDb file the lecture measured 0.084 s before the index and 0.01 s after.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM "movies" WHERE "title" = 'Cars'`

```text
SEARCH movies USING INDEX title_index (title=?)
```

</details>

## M4-E02

**Which columns should be indexed for the Tom Hanks query?** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L405-447](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Perhaps two separate indexes.”*, [lecture5 L338-348](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“will automatically create an index via which I can search for a primary key”*

```sql
CREATE INDEX "person_index" ON "stars" ("person_id");
CREATE INDEX "name_index" ON "people" ("name");
```

**Why:** `movies` is searched by `id`, its INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, which is always indexed for free.
Note that `name_index` is reported as a *covering* index: the query needs only `people.id`, which every index entry already carries (rowid).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT "title" FROM "movies" WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "movie_id" FROM "stars" WHERE "person_id" = (SELECT "id" FROM "people" WHERE "name" = 'Tom Hanks'))`

```text
SEARCH movies USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?) | LIST SUBQUERY 2 | SEARCH stars USING INDEX person_index (person_id=?) | SCALAR SUBQUERY 1 | SEARCH people USING COVERING INDEX name_index (name=?)
```

</details>

## M4-E03

**Make the stars index covering** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L499-542](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Now I have two covering indexes.”*, [lecture5 L482-496](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“It's one in which the query data can be found only by searching the index.”*

```text
SEARCH movies USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?) | LIST SUBQUERY 2 | SEARCH stars USING COVERING INDEX person_index (person_id=?) | SCALAR SUBQUERY 1 | SEARCH people USING COVERING INDEX name_index (name=?)
```

## M4-E04

**A partial index for recent movies** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L892-924](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Now though I'm using 1998, which were rows that were not”*


## M4-E06

**Alice pays Bob $10, atomically** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L1201-1230](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“So this is the atomicity part of transactions.”*

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = "balance" + 10 WHERE "id" = 2;
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = "balance" - 10 WHERE "id" = 1;
COMMIT;
```

**Why:** Atomicity: a second terminal sees the old balances until COMMIT, then both changes at once (L1201-1230).
The checker also fails your answer if you leave the transaction open.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT * FROM "accounts"`

| id | name | balance |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alice | 0 |
| 2 | Bob | 30 |
| 3 | Charlie | 30 |

</details>

## M4-E07

**Roll back a transfer that breaks a constraint** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L1309-1325](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“ROLLBACK like this, hit Enter”*, [lecture5 L1292-1296](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“A rollback only works while we're inside of a transaction.”*

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = "balance" + 10 WHERE "id" = 2;
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = "balance" - 10 WHERE "id" = 1;
ROLLBACK;
```

**Why:** ROLLBACK only works inside a transaction. Without BEGIN, the lecturer had to "undo" Bob's credit by hand with another UPDATE (L1289-1305).
This is Consistency in ACID: the database never ends in a state that violates its constraints.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT * FROM "accounts"`

| id | name | balance |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alice | 0 |
| 2 | Bob | 30 |
| 3 | Charlie | 30 |

</details>

## M4-E08

**Defuse the race condition** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L1337-1388](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Charlie opened up his bank account”*, [lecture5 L1397-1430](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“and the word for this”*

```sql
-- Model answer:
-- 1. Both transfers read Charlie's balance (30) before either one subtracts. Both credit Alice $30,
--    so Alice sees $60 and withdraws it before the bank notices Charlie couldn't cover the second.
-- 2. Make each transfer one transaction and process transactions sequentially (isolated):
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
-- (application checks: SELECT "balance" FROM "accounts" WHERE "id" = 3;  -> must be >= 30)
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = "balance" + 30 WHERE "id" = 1;
UPDATE "accounts" SET "balance" = "balance" - 30 WHERE "id" = 3;
COMMIT;
-- The second transfer starts after the first committed, sees Charlie at $0, and its debit violates
-- CHECK("balance" >= 0), so it is rolled back. Property: Isolation (with Consistency enforced by the CHECK).
```

**Why:** The exclusive lock taken by a writing transaction is what makes the transactions happen one after another (see M4-E09).

## M4-E09

**Lab: see an exclusive lock block a reader** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L1534-1546](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“Runtime error--”*, [lecture5 L1464-1494](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“unlocked, shared, and exclusive”*

```sql
-- connection A
BEGIN EXCLUSIVE TRANSACTION;
-- connection B
SELECT * FROM "accounts";   -- Runtime error: database is locked
-- connection A
COMMIT;
-- connection B
SELECT * FROM "accounts";   -- works again
```

**Why:** SHARED locks let many readers in at once. An EXCLUSIVE lock blocks everyone else. In SQLite the lock covers the whole database file (the coarsest granularity).

**Lab: VACUUM gives space back** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L991-1010](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“We're down to in this case 100 million after dropping our indexes”*

```sql

```

## M4-E11

**Lab: time a query before and after an index** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L127-148](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“I'll say .timer on to make sure that I time my future queries.”*

```sql
.timer on
SELECT * FROM "movies" WHERE "title" = 'Cars';      -- e.g. Run Time: real 0.03x
CREATE INDEX "title_index" ON "movies" ("title");
SELECT * FROM "movies" WHERE "title" = 'Cars';      -- e.g. Run Time: real 0.000x
```

**Why:** real = stopwatch time, user = CPU time spent on the query, sys = time spent in the operating system (the lecture loosely calls it waiting for other processes).

## M4-E12

**Walk the B-tree to find Turning Red** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L782-809](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“How could I find Turning Red?”*, [lecture5 L624-648](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“I've broken that relationship”*, [lecture5 L848-861](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“So these trade-offs are something you should”*

```sql
-- Model answer:
-- 1. Root: is "Turning Red" before "Frozen"? No. Before "Soul"? No, so follow the third child.
--    Leaf: Toy Story, then Turning Red, found. The index returns the ROW NUMBER (pointer) of Turning Red in the table,
--    which SQLite then uses to fetch the other columns (unless the index is covering).
-- 2. Sorting the table would change which title sits next to which id. Other tables reference those ids, so the
--    primary key would no longer identify the same movie. The index is a sorted COPY instead.
-- 3. Space (the copy plus pointers) and slower writes (every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update the tree).
```

**Why:** Each comparison discards most of the remaining candidates, which is why the search stays fast even with millions of rows.

**An index with the columns backwards** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)

## D4-04

**A transfer that created money** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture5 L1285-1296](../sources/lecture5.txt) *“So I need to undo this but I don't have a transaction here.”*
